resolved_by: The Sentencing Commission resolved the split by amending the Guidelines in 2006 (U.S.S.G. app. C amend. 691), adding Application Note 13 to § 2K2.1 to address the conflict.
issue: Does the Guidelines enhancement for possessing a firearm in connection with another felony apply to a gun the defendant obtained through burglary, where no felony separate from the burglary is involved?

sides.position: The enhancement applies only when a second felony is separated by time or conduct from the felony through which the gun was obtained, so it does not apply to a gun taken in a burglary without a separate felony.
cases: United States v. Brake, 904 F.3d 97 (1st Cir. 2018)
United States v. Fenton, 309 F.3d 825 (3d Cir. 2002)
United States v. Szakacs, 212 F.3d 344 (7th Cir. 2000)
United States v. Sanders, 162 F.3d 396 (6th Cir. 1998)

sides.position: The enhancement applies without a separate felony, because a firearm obtained through burglary has the potential of facilitating that burglary.
cases: United States v. Schaal, 340 F.3d 196 (4th Cir. 2003)
United States v. Kenney, 283 F.3d 934 (8th Cir. 2002)
United States v. Luna, 165 F.3d 316 (5th Cir. 1999)

this_court: The Tenth Circuit, in United States v. Mims, No. 25-5139 (10th Cir. 2026), holds the enhancement applies to the stolen firearm, following the Commission's 2006 amendment and the broader reading of Application Note 13.
quote: The Sentencing Commission amended the Guidelines in 2006 to include these Application Notes to address a circuit split about whether the § 2K2.1(b)(7)(B) enhancement applied to firearms obtained through burglary.
cite: United States v. Mims, No. 25-5139 (10th Cir. 2026)
